newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania leaders at odds over investment rules.
newsitem.headline: Albania leaders at odds over investment rules.

text.p: Prospects of a speedy solution to Albania's political and economic woes dimmed on Wednesday after the government said it would not approve a presidential decree designed to regulate investment funds.

Western officials said the renewed political infighting just days before a general election was likely to prolong the economic pain caused by the collapse of five pyramid schemes earlier this year and the chaos that followed their demise.
Thousands of people lost their life-savings in the failed schemes and some 1,500 people were killed in the ensuing unrest.

"We have offered all the help we can give to help Albania resolve the pyramid scheme problem," one senior diplomat told Reuters. "We need to be clear that we're standing on very firm legal ground with all this money involved."

President Sali Berisha, responding to urgent pleas from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank, on Monday signed legislation aimed at controlling the schemes and quelling social unrest in the Balkan nation.

But Finance Minister Arben Malaj, a member of the Socialist Party challenging Berisha's Democratic Party in Sunday's poll, told a news conference the government had no intention of signing the decree, which requires Socialist Prime Minister Bashkim Fino's approval to become valid.
The Socialists currently lead a multi-party interim government formed in March. Malaj said Berisha had altered several key aspects of the draft presented by the government.
"We cannot sign the decree which (represents) a change from the original draft presented by the government. All the changes should first be approved by the government," he said.

The decree was aimed at establishing clearer rules for investment funds and monitoring their activities. It also provided for domestic and international experts to audit the accounts of at least four such schemes still in operation.
"Effective action on the pyramid schemes is an absolute priority," the diplomat said. He added that this was a key condition for international lending to Europe's poorest country to resume.
The breakdown of the five pyramid schemes, which relied on new investors to pay sky-high interest rates to existing depositors, wiped out at least $1.2 billion in savings.
Malaj said there was little chance the political stand-off could be resolved before Sunday's elections, widely seen as the last hope for restoring peace in the former communist nation.
"There were very good odds to have this law approved before the elections," he said. "But I really cannot be held responsible for the president's actions."

Malaj said Berisha had deleted references outlining the exact procedures governing the appointment of the auditors. The president also wanted the finance minister personally to be in charge of monitoring the success of the legislation rather than the government as a whole, he added.

The IMF has promised it would support the government with the selection of international auditors and signalled it would pick up a large part of their bills, but not before authorities have secured a clear framework for the monitoring process.
The IMF has disbursed some $60 million in credits to Albania since 1992, but the programme was suspended in 1995. The World Bank has provided some $300 million in credit lines.
